title: Bruised from the street (Evangelii Gaudium 49)
hookLine: Francis prefers a Church bruised from going out to one that's safe and closed
tomorrow: why would a pope say time is greater than space?

cards: Cleats tell on you. Grass stains on the toes, mud dried into the studs, a scuff from somebody's heel. A pair that's never been worn is spotless, and it hasn't been anywhere.
Pope Francis drew two churches like that, in Evangelii Gaudium, The Joy of the Gospel, a letter to the whole Church. One has been out on the streets all day and comes home bruised, hurting and dirty.
The other stayed in, safe, holding tight to its own security, and it's grown sick from being shut up indoors. He says which one he prefers.

teach.b: He says it in the first person: I prefer the bruised one. The line sits inside a call to go out and offer everyone the life of Jesus Christ.
He doesn't want a Church so worried about being at the center that it gets caught in a web of obsessions and procedures.

Then he names what should trouble us more than our own mistakes: brothers and sisters living without the strength, light and comfort of friendship with Jesus, with no community of faith to hold them up, and no meaning or goal in life.
And he lists what he fears more than going astray. Structures that give a false sense of security. Rules that turn us into harsh judges.
Habits that make us feel safe, while people are starving at the door.
All the while, he writes, Jesus keeps saying, give them something to eat. Those words come from Mark's Gospel, when a hungry crowd has followed Jesus to a lonely place. So the bruise isn't the goal.
It's only the mark of having gone out.
A closed door keeps you clean. It also keeps everyone else outside.

how: Parishes and groups who take Evangelii Gaudium to heart speak of being a Church that goes out: visiting, feeding and welcoming people beyond their own doors.

games.q: what does “bruised from the street” mean?
o: worn out from too many rules and long meetings
hurt from going out to people, rather than staying safe
a Church that was attacked and beaten by its enemies

s: Francis praises a Church that gets hurt because suffering is the goal
the bruise isn't the goal; it's the mark of having gone out.
Francis says he prefers the bruised Church in the first person
I prefer, he writes, not a softer 'one might prefer.'
the danger Francis fears most is making mistakes
he fears more being shut in false security, harsh rules and safe habits while people starve at the door.

games.q: your youth group can keep its cozy Friday hangout, or move it once a month to help at a crowded soup kitchen where things get messy. what would Evangelii Gaudium lean toward?
o: keep the hangout; a safe group is a healthy group.
go out, even if it's messy and someone gets it wrong.
wait until the group is ready and has a perfect plan.
games.why: Francis prefers a Church bruised from going out to one sick from staying in. the mess is the mark of having gone.

practice: Stand, if you can, and press your feet into the floor through your shoes. Feel where the soles are worn: every scuff is a place you went.
Stay with that pressure, and let one door come to mind that you usually keep shut, a neighbor, a coworker who eats alone, a call you keep putting off.

wordCard.voice: Bruised from the street. Francis's picture of a Church that goes out and gets hurt, which he prefers to one that stays safe and closed.

orig.note: Latin: the joy of the Gospel, the first words and title of Francis's exhortation.

carryVoice: Your line: bruised, not closed. The scuffs are just the record of going out. See you tomorrow.
